analysis.one_liner: Bars drug makers from unjustifiably raising prices more than 10% a year on federally covered drugs.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban drug price gouging never got a hearing or vote; the Senate adjourned with it still sitting in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The CURE High Drug Prices Act would have made it illegal for drug makers to raise prices on federally covered prescription drugs in ways that cannot be justified by higher production costs and that patients cannot avoid because of a lack of competition. Price increases of 10% in a year, 20% in three years, or 30% in five years would create a presumption of gouging. The Health and Human Services Secretary could order manufacturers to refund patients and insurers the excessive amounts, and repeat or knowing violators could face penalties of up to triple the excess. The bill was referred to the Senate health committee and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who take prescription drugs covered by Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal health programs, along with the insurers and government programs that pay the bills. The bill would give the federal government a tool to force refunds when a drug maker raises prices sharply without a cost justification, and courts could enforce those orders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients on federally covered prescription drugs

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for manufacturers to raise prices on federally covered drugs in substantial excess of justified production-cost increases, where competition does not let consumers switch to a cheaper alternative [S3].
Creates bright-line presumptions of gouging when prices rise 10% in 12 months, 20% in 36 months, or 30% in 60 months, so patients and regulators do not have to prove intent case by case [S3].

Lets the Health and Human Services Secretary require manufacturers to justify sharp increases, order refunds of the excessive amounts paid by consumers and third-party payors, cap future prices for up to a year, and impose penalties of up to three times the excess for knowing or repeat violations [S3].
Allows the Attorney General to subpoena records and sue manufacturers in federal court when they do not comply with the Secretary's orders [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Prescription drug manufacturers whose price increases on federally covered drugs exceed the bill's thresholds and cannot be justified by production costs or access-expansion spending. They could face refunds of the excess amounts, temporary price caps, and penalties of up to triple the overcharge.

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on the Secretary of Health and Human Services to decide which price increases are 'reasonably justified,' which would put enormous enforcement discretion in one executive agency and invite litigation over every determination [S3].

It only covers drugs whose prices are measured under the federal average manufacturer price rules or wholesale acquisition cost, and only those covered by federal health programs, leaving cash-pay and purely private-market drugs untouched [S3].

Supporters of drug makers would argue that price controls on new medicines could reduce the revenue that funds research into new drugs; the bill itself contains no provision addressing innovation costs beyond a manufacturer's ability to cite access-expansion spending in its justification [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give patients and payers a direct remedy against some of the most extreme drug price increases, with refund and penalty powers that go further than most drug-price proposals. The trade-offs are real but modest: enforcement would hinge on one agency's judgment, coverage is limited to federally priced drugs, and the pharmaceutical industry would argue the penalty structure discourages investment in new medicines. On balance the costs fall on a concentrated industry while the benefits are broad, though the practical effect depends entirely on how aggressively future administrations enforced it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the 115th Congress, referred to the Senate health committee, and died there without a hearing or a vote when that Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Blumenthal introduced the bill with Democratic Sens. Harris, Merkley, and Klobuchar on December 13, 2018, three weeks before the Congress ended [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no further action on it before the 115th Congress adjourned on January 3, 2019 [S5].
No committee hearing, markup, floor vote, or House companion action appears anywhere in the bill's action history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prescription drug manufacturers are better off: no federal prohibition on sharp, unjustified price increases for federally covered drugs took effect, so steep price hikes remain legal. The bill had three cosponsors and no committee action, so no voting bloc's opposition is documented in the record; the outcome reflects inaction rather than a recorded defeat.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers facing no federal price-gouging ban

for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the CURE High Drug Prices Act on December 13, 2018

for.name: Sens. Kamala Harris, Jeff Merkley, and Amy Klobuchar

sides.party_line_note: The bill's four supporters were all Democrats, and no Republican sponsor or cosponsor appears in the record; no vote was ever taken, so no one publicly opposed it on the record.

industries.note: The bill directly targets manufacturers who raise prices on federally covered drugs beyond cost justification, threatening refunds, temporary price caps, and penalties up to triple the overcharge. Because patients cannot shop around when a drug has no competition, the industry's interest in unlimited pricing runs against patients' interest in affordable medicine.

The bill treats third-party payors as consumers entitled to refunds of excessive amounts, so insurers paying drug bills would recover money alongside patients. Their gain tracks the public's gain here.
